entries.snippet:
OpenAI has launched an App Directory for ChatGPT, providing users with a centralized platform to browse and use various tools, alongside opening its SDK to developers for building interactive experiences within the chatbot's UI. This move aligns with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's vision of evolving ChatGPT into a robust platform. The company has also rebranded previously termed "connectors" as "apps," further categorizing them into types such as "apps with file search," "apps with deep research," and "apps with sync."

Some new and expanding ChatGPT apps include integrations with Spotify, now available in the UK, Switzerland, and EU, and new services such as Apple Music and DoorDash. These apps allow users to perform tasks like playlist management and turning meal planning into shopping carts directly through ChatGPT. While it's unclear how these developments will be monetized, OpenAI hints at exploring options like digital goods in the future. Furthermore, data from users may be used to train models if the appropriate settings are enabled, extending across Free to Pro user tiers.

## 05/09/2026 18:24 — Straight Answer

**Yes — OpenAI DOES have a marketplace now.** I confused this by overqualifying it earlier.

| Question | Straight answer |
|---|---|
| Does OpenAI have something like Salesforce AppExchange / Atlassian Marketplace? | **YES — ChatGPT App Directory** |
| Can outside developers build apps? | **YES** |
| Can developers submit them publicly? | **YES** |
| Can users discover/install them inside ChatGPT? | **YES** |
| Can successful apps be featured/recommended by ChatGPT? | **YES** |
| Is OpenAI currently promising normal marketplace revenue-share/payment to every app developer? | **NO** |
| Can our app lead users into **our own commercial SaaS/business**? | **YES** |
| Is the ecosystem mature like Salesforce/AppExchange yet? | **NO — much earlier stage** |

OpenAI opened developer submissions on **17 December 2025**. Approved apps can appear in the App Directory, and OpenAI says apps that resonate with users can be **featured more prominently or recommended by ChatGPT**. citeturn0search0turn0search1

So **this is a marketplace/distribution opportunity already**. The missing piece is mature builder monetization: OpenAI's current Apps SDK page still says **“Details will be shared in the future”** for monetization. citeturn0search2

### And YES — OpenAI has major partnerships

Not just Microsoft.

**Microsoft** remains a major strategic partner and shareholder. In April 2026, OpenAI and Microsoft amended their agreement: Microsoft remains OpenAI's primary cloud partner, while OpenAI gained greater freedom to serve products through other clouds. citeturn0search5

And this year **Amazon/AWS became a major strategic partner too**. In February 2026, Amazon committed **$50 billion** as part of OpenAI's financing and announced a strategic partnership; by June, OpenAI frontier models and Codex became generally available through AWS. citeturn0search7turn0search11turn0search12

So your comparison is actually useful:

> **Salesforce → AppExchange**  
> **Atlassian/Jira → Marketplace**  
> **Slack → Marketplace**  
> **Microsoft → Marketplace**  
> **ChatGPT → App Directory / emerging app ecosystem**

OpenAI is **not yet at Salesforce Marketplace maturity**, but the direction is unmistakable.

### Your Facebook point

I wouldn't say Facebook became successful **because of Facebook Marketplace**. Facebook was already enormous before Marketplace launched in **2016**.

But the underlying point you're making is important:

**A platform becomes much more defensible when other businesses build businesses on top of it.**

Microsoft did it. Salesforce did it extremely well. Apple and Google did it with mobile apps. Atlassian did it around Jira/Confluence.

OpenAI now appears to be building that layer around ChatGPT.

And there's a potentially powerful difference: users don't necessarily have to think *“I need to visit the app store and search for an app.”* OpenAI says it's experimenting with surfacing relevant apps **inside conversations based on conversational context, app usage and user preferences**. citeturn0search0

That could eventually be enormous.

**User:** “I need to organise my flexible workforce tomorrow.”

**ChatGPT:** relevant workforce app appears.

If our product were there, that's potentially **distribution at the moment of intent**.

### Therefore my answer on AUMNITY TEE changes to this:

**Don't ignore this.**

I would allocate **real TEE to investigating it now**.

But first build **one small AUMNITY app/plugin**, not every product. Test:

**Build → submit → get approved → marketplace listing → observe discovery → acquire users → convert to our SaaS.**

If that works, **then this can become a serious distribution channel across UraiFlow / CGWO / Work Platform / LOS**, rather than us trying to build an audience from zero for every product.

And **the V001 Excel needs a V002 correction/expansion** because the strategic significance of the marketplace/distribution model is understated there. memcite

entries.snippet:
During a session at Express Adda, Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos reflected on the platform's meteoric rise over the past decade, growing from $6.3 billion in revenue and $120 million in profit to $45 billion in revenue and $1 billion in profit, with a $400 billion valuation. He recounted Netflix’s early strategic focus on marketing rather than production or distribution and praised Reed Hastings’ visionary belief in internet-based entertainment during the dial-up era. Sarandos discussed Netflix’s positioning as both "classy and massy," emphasizing the importance of personalization and content discovery through algorithms rather than traditional advertising.

He acknowledged the unique characteristics of the Indian market and Netflix’s efforts to localize content, collaborate with Indian creators, and blend mass appeal with quality storytelling. While Netflix has resisted entering live sports like IPL, it continues to invest in diverse Indian stories. Sarandos shared insights into internal strategic discussions, including an offsite in India with Hastings, and addressed questions about AI’s role in media, content curation, and future acquisition strategies. He also participated in a rapid-fire round discussing Bollywood, favorite shows, and dream intellectual property acquisitions, while underlining Netflix's continued commitment to innovation and impactful storytelling globally.
entries.title: Ted Sarandos at Express Adda: 'Netflix is both classy and massy'

entries.snippet: September 2026 brings a variety of streaming content across major platforms like Netflix, Apple TV, Amazon, HBO Max, Hulu/Disney+, and Peacock, though price hikes continue to challenge consumers. Netflix leads with hits like the second season of Guy Ritchie's "The Gentlemen," a reboot of "A Different World," and new seasons of "The Great British Baking Show" and international dramas. Amazon premieres "Neagley," a spinoff of the popular "Reacher," and acclaimed drama "Sterling Point," alongside "American Classic" starring Kevin Kline. Apple TV features the sixth season of "Slow Horses," plus new projects with Ryan Reynolds, Matthew McConaughey, and Woody Harrelson. Peacock adds "The Traitors" with Alan Cumming and popular sports content but offers limited original programming. Hulu highlights include FX’s "The Drop" and new seasons of "American Horror Story," while Disney+ bundles similar offerings. Paramount's line-up includes new "MobLand" episodes with Tom Hardy and extensive sports coverage. HBO Max is quieter, with Sharon Horgan’s comedy "Youth" and select documentaries. Strategic service rotation or bundling is recommended to stay within a $50 budget, as quality offerings vary by platform. entries.snippet: Uber is shifting its stance on regulation as it faces growing competition from autonomous vehicle providers like Alphabet-owned Waymo. While once infamous for dodging regulators, Uber is now aligning with U.S. trade unions to push for stricter rules on robotaxis, advocating for "hybrid" networks combining human drivers and automated taxis. This change reflects Uber’s commercial interests rather than a newfound embrace of stakeholder capitalism. As a major player in the ride-hailing industry with over 10.2 million active drivers and couriers, Uber sees autonomous vehicles as a threat to its dominant market position. With Waymo needing only passengers for its robotaxis, Uber's competitive moat—its driver network—could be undermined. Despite strong business growth and projected cash flows of over $20 billion by 2030, Uber's shares are down 8% in 2026, underscoring investor concerns. The company’s inconsistency—promoting robotaxis in the UK while opposing them in the U.S.—highlights the delicate balance it must manage across diverse markets. Ultimately, Uber's advocacy reflects prioritization of shareholder interests, even as it navigates regulatory challenges and evolving technology landscapes.
entries.title: Uber picks a side in driver vs robotaxi wars: its own

entries.snippet: Uber has unexpectedly aligned with drivers' unions to slow the rollout of autonomous robotaxis, particularly targeting competitors like Alphabet's Waymo. Historically opposed to regulation and labor advocacy, Uber is now lobbying for regulations that mandate hybrid ride-hailing networks, combining human and self-driving services. The shift comes amid rising competition, declining driver earnings in cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco, and investor pressure on Uber to secure its position in the developing autonomous vehicle (AV) market. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, who previously sold Uber's self-driving unit and is restructuring the company by cutting 3,300 jobs, supports AVs but argues the transition should protect current drivers. Uber has proposed and backed legislation in places like New Jersey and Washington DC to restrict AV deployment and promote employment protections. Despite its new stance, labor groups remain skeptical, citing Uber’s past aggressive tactics and inconsistent support across U.S. states. Uber aims to "fragment the market" by partnering with several AV players to retain its role as a ride aggregator. While Waymo opposes hybrid mandates and promotes its own app-based service, both companies acknowledge the need for policy frameworks that balance innovation with labor and safety concerns.
entries.title: Uber and Big Taxi unite in battle against Waymo

entries.snippet: For the first time, Microsoft disclosed quarterly sales figures for its Azure cloud computing unit, highlighting its standing in the competitive cloud market against Amazon and Google. In the most recent quarter, Azure generated $29.4 billion in sales and $101.9 billion for the fiscal year ending June 30. This positions Microsoft behind Amazon Web Services (AWS), which reported $42.2 billion in quarterly cloud sales and $128.7 billion for calendar 2025, but ahead of Google, which posted $24.8 billion in cloud sales in its latest quarter. As part of a broader financial reporting change, Microsoft is transitioning from three segments to two: "Agents and Infra," encompassing cloud and AI-based services, and "Devices and Consumer," covering its Windows OS, Xbox, and advertising operations. CEO Satya Nadella emphasized AI's transformative impact on business and technology. Microsoft also slightly revised its Azure revenue forecast, reallocating some GitHub-associated sales to its M365 Cloud unit. Despite the change, the company maintained its overall quarterly outlook. The move comes amid growing competition in AI and cloud computing, notably as OpenAI broadens its provider base beyond its initial exclusive partnership with Microsoft. Following the announcement, Microsoft shares rose 1.4% in after-hours trading.
entries.title: Microsoft reveals Azure cloud sales in financial reporting shift

entries.snippet: The attempted acquisition of PayPal by Stripe, in partnership with Advent International, ultimately collapsed due to disagreements over PayPal's valuation. Stripe's $60.50 per share offer was based on PayPal's market value before rumors of the deal surfaced. However, once PayPal reported strong Q2 earnings, its share price rose, leading to divergent views on its true worth between the negotiating parties. Although discussions persisted for a month after earnings were released, both sides stood firm on differing interpretations of the stock's rising value. While a revival of the deal remains a remote possibility, future strategies may include PayPal selling off noncore assets. The deal would have marked the largest merger in the payments sector but failed primarily due to disputes over pricing.
entries.title: Why the PayPal takeover fell apart

entries.snippet:
In its 2026 report card, Tom’s Guide evaluates Netflix's performance across several critical categories, concluding with an overall grade of B-. While Netflix remains one of the most popular streaming services, with 72% of U.S. adults using it, rising costs and mixed original content impact its value proposition. The service offers three pricing tiers ranging from $8.99 to $26.99 per month, with the ad-supported Standard plan presenting the best value.

Netflix maintains a strong, frequently refreshed content library, successfully timed around viewer interests and seasonal themes. Its original TV shows, including hits like “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” continue to perform well. However, original movies lag in quality and excitement, dragging down its content score.

The interface remains user-friendly but has seen changes—like removing the Netflix Original badge—that detract from streamlined browsing. The company’s expansion into live content, such as NFL and MLB broadcasts, enhances its appeal, although it doesn't yet rival dedicated live TV services.

Despite its continued relevance and weekly new releases, Netflix faces increasing competition from more affordable and potentially superior alternatives like HBO Max. It remains a staple for regular viewers, but it’s no longer the default choice for all consumers.
entries.title: Netflix Report Card 2026: Is the world's biggest streaming service still worth it?

Uber has proposed and backed legislation in places like New Jersey and Washington DC to restrict AV deployment and promote employment protections. Despite its new stance, labor groups remain skeptical, citing Uber’s past aggressive tactics and inconsistent support across U.S. states. Uber aims to "fragment the market" by partnering with several AV players to retain its role as a ride aggregator. While Waymo opposes hybrid mandates and promotes its own app-based service, both companies acknowledge the need for policy frameworks that balance innovation with labor and safety concerns.
entries.title: Uber and Big Taxi unite in battle against Waymo

entries.snippet: For the first time, Microsoft disclosed quarterly sales figures for its Azure cloud computing unit, highlighting its standing in the competitive cloud market against Amazon and Google. In the most recent quarter, Azure generated $29.4 billion in sales and $101.9 billion for the fiscal year ending June 30. This positions Microsoft behind Amazon Web Services (AWS), which reported $42.2 billion in quarterly cloud sales and $128.7 billion for calendar 2025, but ahead of Google, which posted $24.8 billion in cloud sales in its latest quarter. As part of a broader financial reporting change, Microsoft is transitioning from three segments to two: "Agents and Infra," encompassing cloud and AI-based services, and "Devices and Consumer," covering its Windows OS, Xbox, and advertising operations. CEO Satya Nadella emphasized AI's transformative impact on business and technology. Microsoft also slightly revised its Azure revenue forecast, reallocating some GitHub-associated sales to its M365 Cloud unit. Despite the change, the company maintained its overall quarterly outlook. The move comes amid growing competition in AI and cloud computing, notably as OpenAI broadens its provider base beyond its initial exclusive partnership with Microsoft. Following the announcement, Microsoft shares rose 1.4% in after-hours trading.
entries.title: Microsoft reveals Azure cloud sales in financial reporting shift

entries.snippet: The attempted acquisition of PayPal by Stripe, in partnership with Advent International, ultimately collapsed due to disagreements over PayPal's valuation. Stripe's $60.50 per share offer was based on PayPal's market value before rumors of the deal surfaced. However, once PayPal reported strong Q2 earnings, its share price rose, leading to divergent views on its true worth between the negotiating parties. Although discussions persisted for a month after earnings were released, both sides stood firm on differing interpretations of the stock's rising value. While a revival of the deal remains a remote possibility, future strategies may include PayPal selling off noncore assets. The deal would have marked the largest merger in the payments sector but failed primarily due to disputes over pricing.
entries.title: Why the PayPal takeover fell apart

entries.snippet:
In its 2026 report card, Tom’s Guide evaluates Netflix's performance across several critical categories, concluding with an overall grade of B-. While Netflix remains one of the most popular streaming services, with 72% of U.S. adults using it, rising costs and mixed original content impact its value proposition. The service offers three pricing tiers ranging from $8.99 to $26.99 per month, with the ad-supported Standard plan presenting the best value.

Netflix maintains a strong, frequently refreshed content library, successfully timed around viewer interests and seasonal themes. Its original TV shows, including hits like “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” continue to perform well. However, original movies lag in quality and excitement, dragging down its content score.

The interface remains user-friendly but has seen changes—like removing the Netflix Original badge—that detract from streamlined browsing. The company’s expansion into live content, such as NFL and MLB broadcasts, enhances its appeal, although it doesn't yet rival dedicated live TV services.

Despite its continued relevance and weekly new releases, Netflix faces increasing competition from more affordable and potentially superior alternatives like HBO Max. It remains a staple for regular viewers, but it’s no longer the default choice for all consumers.
entries.title: Netflix Report Card 2026: Is the world's biggest streaming service still worth it?

## 05/09/2026 17:26 — OpenAI App Marketplace Research

Yes — **I should have surfaced this earlier** when we were discussing building products and ways software builders could make money. The important opportunity is not merely “make a GPT”; OpenAI has been moving toward a **platform/ecosystem model where third-party software, workflows, data and actions live inside ChatGPT/Codex**.

But one correction is important: it **didn't suddenly change after February 2026**. The sequence is:

**GPT Store — 10 Jan 2024 → Apps SDK — 6 Oct 2025 → developer App Directory — 17 Dec 2025 → Plugin Directory — 9 Jul 2026.** The July 2026 change is significant because a plugin can now package **skills + apps + app templates**, and the Plugin Directory spans ChatGPT and Codex. citeturn576613search9turn576613search0turn576613search1turn388243search1

And I would **not yet describe it as “OpenAI lets everyone build apps and shares money with them.”** OpenAI announced GPT-builder engagement payments back in 2024, but the current Apps SDK documentation still says monetization details will be shared in the future. Developers can, however, connect an app to their **own backend and premium product**, which means the stronger business model today is to own the SaaS/product revenue yourself and use ChatGPT/Plugins as a distribution and interaction channel. citeturn576613search9turn576613search4turn576613search0

### V001 Excel completed

I built the requested research workbook with **15 structured sheets**, including version control, context/evidence rules, OpenAI historical evolution, current plugin/app architecture, marketplace sizes, top apps, OpenAI launch products, technology, security/constraints, monetization, build-time/team/cost model, opportunity analysis, field dictionary and a full source register.

Some useful market-size findings captured inside it include **Zapier 9,000+ apps**, **Salesforce AppExchange ~5,000 apps**, **Microsoft 4,000+ AI apps/agents plus 11,000+ models**, **Atlassian 4,000+ apps/integrations**, and **Slack 2,600+ apps**. These aren't perfectly comparable categories, so the workbook explicitly records the counting basis instead of pretending they measure the same thing. citeturn468997search18turn672750search16turn468997search17turn468997search2turn672750search4

The engineering sheet also gives editable **GBP day-rate assumptions and formula-driven low/high build costs** for five levels ranging from a skill-only prototype through an enterprise transactional app. For products such as Canva, Figma, Zillow, Booking.com and Coursera, I separated company economics from **app-specific economics**, because app-development cost/revenue/team numbers generally aren't publicly disclosed. For example, Canva reported **$3.5B 2025 revenue**, Figma **$1.056B**, Zillow **$2.583B**, and Coursera **$757M**—but none of those figures should be mistaken for revenue from their ChatGPT integrations. citeturn461244search3turn469160search1turn469160search2turn461244search10

**File:**  
[Download chatgpt_v001_ai_app_marketplace_product_research_20260905_1726.xlsx](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_ai_app_marketplace_product_research_20260905_1726.xlsx)

The part I would pay particular attention to is **`12_Opportunities`**. The strongest route isn't “build random ChatGPT apps.” It is **own a defensible vertical SaaS/backend, expose it through MCP/apps/plugins, package repeatable expertise as skills, and use ChatGPT/Codex as another user interface and distribution surface**. That keeps the valuable IP with the software company even if OpenAI changes its marketplace packaging again.

## 05/09/2026 18:35 — Social Network Market Wars V001

Created the separate research workbook:

[**Download — chatgpt_v001_social_network_market_wars_20260905_1835.xlsx**](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_social_network_market_wars_20260905_1835.xlsx)

And **your Microsoft/MySpace memory was close, but the transaction was different**:

**Microsoft did not, based on the reliable evidence I found, offer to buy MySpace.** News Corp bought Intermix/MySpace for about **$580M in 2005**. In 2006, MySpace then invited **Microsoft, Google and Yahoo to bid for its search/advertising business**. Google beat Microsoft with a deal guaranteeing at least **$900M** subject to traffic commitments. citeturn0search0turn1search7turn1search0

Interestingly, Microsoft then went with **Facebook**: an advertising partnership in August 2006, followed by a **$240M investment in Facebook at a $15B valuation in October 2007**. citeturn1search12turn0search5

The workbook has **9 sheets** covering the timeline, SixDegrees/Friendster/MySpace/Facebook/Orkut/Microsoft Live Spaces/Bebo comparison, acquisitions versus partnerships, why Facebook won despite much richer competitors, incumbent strategies, lessons for today's AI marketplace battle, sources, version control and field definitions.

The most important sheet for the next page is **`06_AI_Market_Lessons`** — it deliberately connects this history to the question we're really investigating now:

**Could OpenAI vs Claude vs Microsoft/Google/Meta eventually be decided less by who has the best model/more money and more by who creates the strongest users → developers → apps → partners → businesses → marketplace flywheel?**

That is worth studying much more deeply.

entries.snippet:
OpenAI has launched an App Directory for ChatGPT, providing users with a centralized platform to browse and use various tools, alongside opening its SDK to developers for building interactive experiences within the chatbot's UI. This move aligns with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's vision of evolving ChatGPT into a robust platform. The company has also rebranded previously termed "connectors" as "apps," further categorizing them into types such as "apps with file search," "apps with deep research," and "apps with sync."

Some new and expanding ChatGPT apps include integrations with Spotify, now available in the UK, Switzerland, and EU, and new services such as Apple Music and DoorDash. These apps allow users to perform tasks like playlist management and turning meal planning into shopping carts directly through ChatGPT. While it's unclear how these developments will be monetized, OpenAI hints at exploring options like digital goods in the future. Furthermore, data from users may be used to train models if the appropriate settings are enabled, extending across Free to Pro user tiers.

The scope is broader than just “technology history.” I’m treating each file as a **competitive-market case study**: who was first, who had the money, who bought whom, what distribution advantage mattered, when a marketplace/ecosystem appeared, why a late entrant won or failed, and what that teaches us about today’s OpenAI/Claude/Google/Microsoft/Meta platform race.

I’m also keeping the files independent rather than putting 10 markets into one workbook. That way you can open **one separate ChatGPT page per market**, attach only that V001 file, and continue the research without mixing contexts.

entries.snippet:
During a session at Express Adda, Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos reflected on the platform's meteoric rise over the past decade, growing from $6.3 billion in revenue and $120 million in profit to $45 billion in revenue and $1 billion in profit, with a $400 billion valuation. He recounted Netflix’s early strategic focus on marketing rather than production or distribution and praised Reed Hastings’ visionary belief in internet-based entertainment during the dial-up era. Sarandos discussed Netflix’s positioning as both "classy and massy," emphasizing the importance of personalization and content discovery through algorithms rather than traditional advertising.

He acknowledged the unique characteristics of the Indian market and Netflix’s efforts to localize content, collaborate with Indian creators, and blend mass appeal with quality storytelling. While Netflix has resisted entering live sports like IPL, it continues to invest in diverse Indian stories. Sarandos shared insights into internal strategic discussions, including an offsite in India with Hastings, and addressed questions about AI’s role in media, content curation, and future acquisition strategies. He also participated in a rapid-fire round discussing Bollywood, favorite shows, and dream intellectual property acquisitions, while underlining Netflix's continued commitment to innovation and impactful storytelling globally.
entries.title: Ted Sarandos at Express Adda: 'Netflix is both classy and massy'

entries.snippet: September 2026 brings a variety of streaming content across major platforms like Netflix, Apple TV, Amazon, HBO Max, Hulu/Disney+, and Peacock, though price hikes continue to challenge consumers. Netflix leads with hits like the second season of Guy Ritchie's "The Gentlemen," a reboot of "A Different World," and new seasons of "The Great British Baking Show" and international dramas. Amazon premieres "Neagley," a spinoff of the popular "Reacher," and acclaimed drama "Sterling Point," alongside "American Classic" starring Kevin Kline. Apple TV features the sixth season of "Slow Horses," plus new projects with Ryan Reynolds, Matthew McConaughey, and Woody Harrelson. Peacock adds "The Traitors" with Alan Cumming and popular sports content but offers limited original programming. Hulu highlights include FX’s "The Drop" and new seasons of "American Horror Story," while Disney+ bundles similar offerings. Paramount's line-up includes new "MobLand" episodes with Tom Hardy and extensive sports coverage. HBO Max is quieter, with Sharon Horgan’s comedy "Youth" and select documentaries. Strategic service rotation or bundling is recommended to stay within a $50 budget, as quality offerings vary by platform. entries.snippet: Uber is shifting its stance on regulation as it faces growing competition from autonomous vehicle providers like Alphabet-owned Waymo. While once infamous for dodging regulators, Uber is now aligning with U.S. trade unions to push for stricter rules on robotaxis, advocating for "hybrid" networks combining human drivers and automated taxis. This change reflects Uber’s commercial interests rather than a newfound embrace of stakeholder capitalism. As a major player in the ride-hailing industry with over 10.2 million active drivers and couriers, Uber sees autonomous vehicles as a threat to its dominant market position. With Waymo needing only passengers for its robotaxis, Uber's competitive moat—its driver network—could be undermined. Despite strong business growth and projected cash flows of over $20 billion by 2030, Uber's shares are down 8% in 2026, underscoring investor concerns. The company’s inconsistency—promoting robotaxis in the UK while opposing them in the U.S.—highlights the delicate balance it must manage across diverse markets. Ultimately, Uber's advocacy reflects prioritization of shareholder interests, even as it navigates regulatory challenges and evolving technology landscapes.
entries.title: Uber picks a side in driver vs robotaxi wars: its own

entries.snippet: Uber has unexpectedly aligned with drivers' unions to slow the rollout of autonomous robotaxis, particularly targeting competitors like Alphabet's Waymo. Historically opposed to regulation and labor advocacy, Uber is now lobbying for regulations that mandate hybrid ride-hailing networks, combining human and self-driving services. The shift comes amid rising competition, declining driver earnings in cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco, and investor pressure on Uber to secure its position in the developing autonomous vehicle (AV) market. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, who previously sold Uber's self-driving unit and is restructuring the company by cutting 3,300 jobs, supports AVs but argues the transition should protect current drivers. Uber has proposed and backed legislation in places like New Jersey and Washington DC to restrict AV deployment and promote employment protections. Despite its new stance, labor groups remain skeptical, citing Uber’s past aggressive tactics and inconsistent support across U.S. states. Uber aims to "fragment the market" by partnering with several AV players to retain its role as a ride aggregator. While Waymo opposes hybrid mandates and promotes its own app-based service, both companies acknowledge the need for policy frameworks that balance innovation with labor and safety concerns.
entries.title: Uber and Big Taxi unite in battle against Waymo

entries.snippet: For the first time, Microsoft disclosed quarterly sales figures for its Azure cloud computing unit, highlighting its standing in the competitive cloud market against Amazon and Google. In the most recent quarter, Azure generated $29.4 billion in sales and $101.9 billion for the fiscal year ending June 30. This positions Microsoft behind Amazon Web Services (AWS), which reported $42.2 billion in quarterly cloud sales and $128.7 billion for calendar 2025, but ahead of Google, which posted $24.8 billion in cloud sales in its latest quarter. As part of a broader financial reporting change, Microsoft is transitioning from three segments to two: "Agents and Infra," encompassing cloud and AI-based services, and "Devices and Consumer," covering its Windows OS, Xbox, and advertising operations. CEO Satya Nadella emphasized AI's transformative impact on business and technology. Microsoft also slightly revised its Azure revenue forecast, reallocating some GitHub-associated sales to its M365 Cloud unit. Despite the change, the company maintained its overall quarterly outlook. The move comes amid growing competition in AI and cloud computing, notably as OpenAI broadens its provider base beyond its initial exclusive partnership with Microsoft. Following the announcement, Microsoft shares rose 1.4% in after-hours trading.
entries.title: Microsoft reveals Azure cloud sales in financial reporting shift

entries.snippet: The attempted acquisition of PayPal by Stripe, in partnership with Advent International, ultimately collapsed due to disagreements over PayPal's valuation. Stripe's $60.50 per share offer was based on PayPal's market value before rumors of the deal surfaced. However, once PayPal reported strong Q2 earnings, its share price rose, leading to divergent views on its true worth between the negotiating parties. Although discussions persisted for a month after earnings were released, both sides stood firm on differing interpretations of the stock's rising value. While a revival of the deal remains a remote possibility, future strategies may include PayPal selling off noncore assets. The deal would have marked the largest merger in the payments sector but failed primarily due to disputes over pricing.
entries.title: Why the PayPal takeover fell apart

entries.snippet:
In its 2026 report card, Tom’s Guide evaluates Netflix's performance across several critical categories, concluding with an overall grade of B-. While Netflix remains one of the most popular streaming services, with 72% of U.S. adults using it, rising costs and mixed original content impact its value proposition. The service offers three pricing tiers ranging from $8.99 to $26.99 per month, with the ad-supported Standard plan presenting the best value.

Netflix maintains a strong, frequently refreshed content library, successfully timed around viewer interests and seasonal themes. Its original TV shows, including hits like “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” continue to perform well. However, original movies lag in quality and excitement, dragging down its content score.

The interface remains user-friendly but has seen changes—like removing the Netflix Original badge—that detract from streamlined browsing. The company’s expansion into live content, such as NFL and MLB broadcasts, enhances its appeal, although it doesn't yet rival dedicated live TV services.

Despite its continued relevance and weekly new releases, Netflix faces increasing competition from more affordable and potentially superior alternatives like HBO Max. It remains a staple for regular viewers, but it’s no longer the default choice for all consumers.
entries.title: Netflix Report Card 2026: Is the world's biggest streaming service still worth it?

Created **10 separate V001 Excel workbooks**, each designed to become its own future research page. They all use the same structure as the social-network workbook: dashboard, timeline, product/company comparison, acquisitions/partnerships, why winners won, AI-market lessons, sources, field dictionary, and version control.

10. [Enterprise SaaS Platform Wars](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_enterprise_saas_platform_wars_20260905_1940.xlsx)

### Particularly relevant to our OpenAI/Claude question

The **three I would study first** are:

**Smartphone/Mobile OS** — because Apple/Android show how **App Store + developers + users + payments + distribution** can destroy stronger incumbents such as Nokia, BlackBerry and Microsoft.

**Cloud Computing** — because Amazon was *not* an enterprise infrastructure leader, yet AWS beat traditional IT giants by creating a developer platform and ecosystem.

**Enterprise SaaS** — because Salesforce/AppExchange is probably the closest historical analogue to what OpenAI and Claude are now trying to develop through **apps/plugins + partners + consulting firms + customer implementations**.

The files are intentionally **V001 foundations**, so when you open a separate page for one market we can take that one to V002/V003 with much deeper company finances, historic market-share curves, founder decisions, failed acquisition offers, product architecture, team sizes, pricing, network-effect models, partnership economics and explicit parallels to the current AI race.

entries.snippet:
OpenAI has launched an App Directory for ChatGPT, providing users with a centralized platform to browse and use various tools, alongside opening its SDK to developers for building interactive experiences within the chatbot's UI. This move aligns with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's vision of evolving ChatGPT into a robust platform. The company has also rebranded previously termed "connectors" as "apps," further categorizing them into types such as "apps with file search," "apps with deep research," and "apps with sync."

Some new and expanding ChatGPT apps include integrations with Spotify, now available in the UK, Switzerland, and EU, and new services such as Apple Music and DoorDash. These apps allow users to perform tasks like playlist management and turning meal planning into shopping carts directly through ChatGPT. While it's unclear how these developments will be monetized, OpenAI hints at exploring options like digital goods in the future. Furthermore, data from users may be used to train models if the appropriate settings are enabled, extending across Free to Pro user tiers.

entries.snippet:
During a session at Express Adda, Netflix Co-CEO Ted Sarandos reflected on the platform's meteoric rise over the past decade, growing from $6.3 billion in revenue and $120 million in profit to $45 billion in revenue and $1 billion in profit, with a $400 billion valuation. He recounted Netflix’s early strategic focus on marketing rather than production or distribution and praised Reed Hastings’ visionary belief in internet-based entertainment during the dial-up era. Sarandos discussed Netflix’s positioning as both "classy and massy," emphasizing the importance of personalization and content discovery through algorithms rather than traditional advertising.

He acknowledged the unique characteristics of the Indian market and Netflix’s efforts to localize content, collaborate with Indian creators, and blend mass appeal with quality storytelling. While Netflix has resisted entering live sports like IPL, it continues to invest in diverse Indian stories. Sarandos shared insights into internal strategic discussions, including an offsite in India with Hastings, and addressed questions about AI’s role in media, content curation, and future acquisition strategies. He also participated in a rapid-fire round discussing Bollywood, favorite shows, and dream intellectual property acquisitions, while underlining Netflix's continued commitment to innovation and impactful storytelling globally.
entries.title: Ted Sarandos at Express Adda: 'Netflix is both classy and massy'

entries.snippet: September 2026 brings a variety of streaming content across major platforms like Netflix, Apple TV, Amazon, HBO Max, Hulu/Disney+, and Peacock, though price hikes continue to challenge consumers. Netflix leads with hits like the second season of Guy Ritchie's "The Gentlemen," a reboot of "A Different World," and new seasons of "The Great British Baking Show" and international dramas. Amazon premieres "Neagley," a spinoff of the popular "Reacher," and acclaimed drama "Sterling Point," alongside "American Classic" starring Kevin Kline. Apple TV features the sixth season of "Slow Horses," plus new projects with Ryan Reynolds, Matthew McConaughey, and Woody Harrelson. Peacock adds "The Traitors" with Alan Cumming and popular sports content but offers limited original programming. Hulu highlights include FX’s "The Drop" and new seasons of "American Horror Story," while Disney+ bundles similar offerings. Paramount's line-up includes new "MobLand" episodes with Tom Hardy and extensive sports coverage. HBO Max is quieter, with Sharon Horgan’s comedy "Youth" and select documentaries. Strategic service rotation or bundling is recommended to stay within a $50 budget, as quality offerings vary by platform. Viewer guidance rates platforms as “play,” “pause,” or “stop” based on content quality and subscription value.

entries.snippet: Uber is shifting its stance on regulation as it faces growing competition from autonomous vehicle providers like Alphabet-owned Waymo. While once infamous for dodging regulators, Uber is now aligning with U.S. trade unions to push for stricter rules on robotaxis, advocating for "hybrid" networks combining human drivers and automated taxis. This change reflects Uber’s commercial interests rather than a newfound embrace of stakeholder capitalism. As a major player in the ride-hailing industry with over 10.2 million active drivers and couriers, Uber sees autonomous vehicles as a threat to its dominant market position. With Waymo needing only passengers for its robotaxis, Uber's competitive moat—its driver network—could be undermined. Despite strong business growth and projected cash flows of over $20 billion by 2030, Uber's shares are down 8% in 2026, underscoring investor concerns. The company’s inconsistency—promoting robotaxis in the UK while opposing them in the U.S.—highlights the delicate balance it must manage across diverse markets. Ultimately, Uber's advocacy reflects prioritization of shareholder interests, even as it navigates regulatory challenges and evolving technology landscapes.
entries.title: Uber picks a side in driver vs robotaxi wars: its own

entries.snippet: Uber has unexpectedly aligned with drivers' unions to slow the rollout of autonomous robotaxis, particularly targeting competitors like Alphabet's Waymo. Historically opposed to regulation and labor advocacy, Uber is now lobbying for regulations that mandate hybrid ride-hailing networks, combining human and self-driving services. The shift comes amid rising competition, declining driver earnings in cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco, and investor pressure on Uber to secure its position in the developing autonomous vehicle (AV) market. CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, who previously sold Uber's self-driving unit and is restructuring the company by cutting 3,300 jobs, supports AVs but argues the transition should protect current drivers. Uber has proposed and backed legislation in places like New Jersey and Washington DC to restrict AV deployment and promote employment protections. Despite its new stance, labor groups remain skeptical, citing Uber’s past aggressive tactics and inconsistent support across U.S. states. Uber aims to "fragment the market" by partnering with several AV players to retain its role as a ride aggregator. While Waymo opposes hybrid mandates and promotes its own app-based service, both companies acknowledge the need for policy frameworks that balance innovation with labor and safety concerns.
entries.title: Uber and Big Taxi unite in battle against Waymo

entries.snippet: For the first time, Microsoft disclosed quarterly sales figures for its Azure cloud computing unit, highlighting its standing in the competitive cloud market against Amazon and Google. In the most recent quarter, Azure generated $29.4 billion in sales and $101.9 billion for the fiscal year ending June 30. This positions Microsoft behind Amazon Web Services (AWS), which reported $42.2 billion in quarterly cloud sales and $128.7 billion for calendar 2025, but ahead of Google, which posted $24.8 billion in cloud sales in its latest quarter. As part of a broader financial reporting change, Microsoft is transitioning from three segments to two: "Agents and Infra," encompassing cloud and AI-based services, and "Devices and Consumer," covering its Windows OS, Xbox, and advertising operations. CEO Satya Nadella emphasized AI's transformative impact on business and technology. Microsoft also slightly revised its Azure revenue forecast, reallocating some GitHub-associated sales to its M365 Cloud unit. Despite the change, the company maintained its overall quarterly outlook. The move comes amid growing competition in AI and cloud computing, notably as OpenAI broadens its provider base beyond its initial exclusive partnership with Microsoft. Following the announcement, Microsoft shares rose 1.4% in after-hours trading.
entries.title: Microsoft reveals Azure cloud sales in financial reporting shift

entries.snippet: The attempted acquisition of PayPal by Stripe, in partnership with Advent International, ultimately collapsed due to disagreements over PayPal's valuation. Stripe's $60.50 per share offer was based on PayPal's market value before rumors of the deal surfaced. However, once PayPal reported strong Q2 earnings, its share price rose, leading to divergent views on its true worth between the negotiating parties. Although discussions persisted for a month after earnings were released, both sides stood firm on differing interpretations of the stock's rising value. While a revival of the deal remains a remote possibility, future strategies may include PayPal selling off noncore assets. The deal would have marked the largest merger in the payments sector but failed primarily due to disputes over pricing.
entries.title: Why the PayPal takeover fell apart

entries.snippet:
In its 2026 report card, Tom’s Guide evaluates Netflix's performance across several critical categories, concluding with an overall grade of B-. While Netflix remains one of the most popular streaming services, with 72% of U.S. adults using it, rising costs and mixed original content impact its value proposition. The service offers three pricing tiers ranging from $8.99 to $26.99 per month, with the ad-supported Standard plan presenting the best value.

Netflix maintains a strong, frequently refreshed content library, successfully timed around viewer interests and seasonal themes. Its original TV shows, including hits like “Stranger Things” and “Wednesday,” continue to perform well. However, original movies lag in quality and excitement, dragging down its content score.

The interface remains user-friendly but has seen changes—like removing the Netflix Original badge—that detract from streamlined browsing. The company’s expansion into live content, such as NFL and MLB broadcasts, enhances its appeal, although it doesn't yet rival dedicated live TV services.

Despite its continued relevance and weekly new releases, Netflix faces increasing competition from more affordable and potentially superior alternatives like HBO Max. It remains a staple for regular viewers, but it’s no longer the default choice for all consumers.
entries.title: Netflix Report Card 2026: Is the world's biggest streaming service still worth it?

Yes — I’ll create **separate V001 research workbooks**, each following the same pattern as the social-network file: timeline, product/company comparison, deals/partnerships, why winners won, why incumbents failed, market-structure lessons, AI-platform analogy, sources, field dictionary, and version control.

I’m going to cover the most useful “platform war” markets separately: **search engines, web browsers, smartphones/mobile OS, messaging, e-commerce/marketplaces, cloud computing, video streaming, ride-hailing, digital payments/fintech, and enterprise SaaS/platform ecosystems**. That gives us 10 independent files you can open as separate research pages later.

One important correction is already clear: this was **not a February 2026 switch**. OpenAI launched the GPT Store in **January 2024**, announced chat-native Apps + Apps SDK on **6 October 2025**, opened the App Directory to developer submissions on **17 December 2025**, and then on **9 July 2026** migrated the App Directory into the broader **Plugin Directory** spanning ChatGPT and Codex. The current plugin packaging can contain **skills, apps, and app templates**. 

The money point also needs a careful distinction: OpenAI promised a GPT-builder usage-based revenue program in 2024, but for the newer Apps SDK the current official documentation still says **monetization details will be shared in the future**. So I’m not going to label the present Plugin Directory as an established “everyone earns from OpenAI” marketplace unless evidence supports it.

## 05/09/2026 19:54 — Current + Future Market Wars

Yes. **The latest major platform war happening right now is the AI Agent Platform war.** It is moving beyond “whose chatbot/model is best?” toward:

**AI → Agent → Tools → Other agents → Marketplace → Payments → Business execution.**

OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google, AWS, Salesforce and ServiceNow are all moving toward agent directories/marketplaces or agent platforms. A July 2026 analysis explicitly describes this as a race to create the **“app stores” of the agentic era**. citeturn0news31

And developments **this week** make the next step clearer: India is preparing agent-authorized UPI payments, while Anthropic has released retailer blueprints for shopping and merchant agents. citeturn0news35turn0news36

So I used the earlier market-war idea and projected it forward into **8 separate future-facing V001 workbooks**:

1. **Most important now — AI Agent Platform Wars**  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_ai_agent_platform_market_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

2. **Agentic Commerce & Payment Wars** — agents buying, UPI/payment delegation, merchant agents, checkout and marketplace routing.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_agentic_commerce_payment_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

3. **AI Coding & Software Factory Wars** — Codex/Claude Code/Copilot and the movement toward autonomous software engineering.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_ai_coding_software_factory_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

4. **Humanoid Robotics Platform Wars** — physical AI, robot operating layers, simulation and eventually robot-skill marketplaces.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_humanoid_robotics_platform_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

5. **Autonomous Vehicle & Mobility Wars** — Waymo/Tesla/Baidu/Zoox and eventually vehicles acting as autonomous economic agents.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_autonomous_vehicle_mobility_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

6. **Spatial Computing & AI Glasses Wars** — Meta/Apple/Google and the possible post-smartphone interface.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_spatial_computing_ai_glasses_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

7. **AI Compute & Chip Platform Wars** — NVIDIA/CUDA versus AMD, Google TPU, AWS Trainium and hyperscaler custom silicon.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_ai_compute_chip_platform_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

8. **AI Agent Governance, Identity & Security Wars** — agent identity, permissions, audit, policy, provenance and kill switches.  
[Download V001](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_v001_ai_governance_identity_security_wars_20260905_1954.xlsx)

### One especially important thing I see

The historical sequence we've now captured across all these files looks something like:

**Internet → Search → Social → Smartphone → App Store → Cloud → SaaS → AI models → AI agents → Agent marketplace → Agent commerce → Physical agents**

The **2026 inflection point appears to be around the bold part:**

### **AI models → agents → marketplaces → transactions**

That's why your earlier Facebook question is actually useful. We shouldn't automatically assume **the company with the richest model or most money wins**. The eventual winner may be the company that gets the strongest flywheel of:

**Users ↔ Agents ↔ Developers ↔ Businesses ↔ Partners ↔ Payments ↔ Data/Workflows**

The recent evidence is already pointing in that direction. citeturn0news31turn0news35

I also deliberately made **future predictions a separate sheet** in every workbook, with horizons and confidence, so when we reopen these in 2027/2028 we can compare **what we predicted vs what actually happened** rather than rewriting history.

I can monitor these emerging platform wars and flag major shifts such as a new marketplace, payment standard, acquisition or clear winner. Want me to set that up?

items.snippet: India is developing a framework to enable AI agents to conduct small digital payments via the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) without requiring approval for each transaction, according to sources familiar with the matter. This initiative positions UPI—a system already recognized as the world’s largest retail fast-payment network by transaction volume—to be among the first national infrastructures globally supporting agentic payments. In August 2026, UPI handled 24.51 billion transactions worth ₹29.82 trillion ($314.21 billion), with Google Pay and PhonePe dominating the volume. The new system, called the Unified Agent Protocol, is expected to debut at the Global Fintech Fest in Mumbai. Initial applications will focus on low-value, routine purchases, with potential for more complex interactions, such as AI-driven investment decisions. The protocol will employ mechanisms like UPI Circle and Reserve Pay, allowing for funds delegation and blocking. NPCI aims to include features like rule-based payments, spending limits, identity checks, and liability provisions. Global firms like Mastercard, Visa, and Pine Labs are also implementing similar technologies in India, highlighting a broader trend toward AI-enabled commerce.

supporting_websites.snippet: Artificial intelligence company Anthropic has launched AI agent blueprints for retailers to develop shopping and merchant agents using its Claude platform. This initiative, announced on September 2, 2026, comes as demand rises for both internal and customer-facing conversational search tools in preparation for the holiday shopping season. The blueprints are designed to assist retailers in implementing advanced AI solutions that enhance online shopping experiences and streamline commercial operations. By equipping businesses with the tools to create tailored AI agents, Anthropic aims to support retailers in boosting engagement and efficiency during one of the busiest retail periods of the year.

## 05/09/2026 18:20 — Is OpenAI App Development Worth Our TEE?

**No, partner — I am NOT saying developing an OpenAI app is useless or that we shouldn't put TEE into it.** I was warning against a *different* thing: spending major TEE building an app **only because we expect OpenAI itself to pay us**.

### 1. Is OpenAI currently paying builders?

There are **two different systems**, and I should have separated them more clearly.

| System | OpenAI pays builder? | Situation |
|---|---|---|
| **Custom GPT / GPT Store** | **Limited/experimental** | OpenAI originally announced usage-based earnings for US GPT builders; it was tested with a small selected group rather than becoming a clearly documented worldwide payout system. citeturn0search0turn0search2 |
| **Apps SDK / Apps / Plugin ecosystem** | **No general OpenAI builder payment model published yet** | Current official documentation literally puts monetization under “Details will be shared in the future.” citeturn0search1 |
| **Our own SaaS connected to ChatGPT** | **YES — customers can pay us** | OpenAI explicitly says an app can connect to our existing backend and, in future, users can sign in/access premium features. citeturn0search1 |
| **Future commerce inside ChatGPT** | Planned | OpenAI says support for Agentic Commerce Protocol / instant checkout is planned. citeturn0search1 |

So **don't build expecting a cheque from OpenAI. Build because ChatGPT can become a distribution/interface channel for OUR paid software.**

---

# 2. Then should we put TEE into OpenAI apps?

### **YES — but architecture matters enormously.**

I would **not** recommend:

> Spend 3 months creating something whose entire intellectual property is just an OpenAI app.

I **would** recommend:

> **AUMNITY product / SaaS core → MCP/API → OpenAI Plugin/App → later Claude/Gemini/Copilot/etc. adapters**

Then our investment isn't lost if OpenAI changes its marketplace.

This is particularly interesting because OpenAI says its Apps SDK is based on **MCP**, is **open source**, and apps built with it can run wherever the standard is adopted. citeturn0search1

That changes my TEE assessment considerably.

### Think of it this way

**Bad investment**

`100% TEE → ChatGPT-specific wrapper → hope OpenAI pays us`

**Potentially excellent investment**

`80–90% TEE → our reusable SaaS/domain engine`

`10–20% TEE → OpenAI App/Plugin/MCP distribution layer`

Then even if the OpenAI marketplace disappears tomorrow, **we still own the product**.

---

# 3. Actually, our existing products may fit this unusually well

For example, we shouldn't create another random *“AI Timesheet GPT.”*

Instead:

**AUMNITY Work Platform**  
→ owns work/tasks/identity/tenancy

**CGWO**  
→ owns planning, capacity, matching, replanning

**UraiFlow**  
→ capture/transcription/extraction

**AT-LOS**  
→ evidence/pattern/context layer

Then an OpenAI plugin could expose controlled workflows such as:

> “What hasn't Subha completed today?”

or

> “Replan today's available workforce.”

or

> “Turn this call transcript into proposed CRM follow-ups.”

or

> “Show me the evidence behind this recommendation.”

The **plugin isn't the product**.

### **Our SaaS is the product. ChatGPT becomes one interface to it.**

That is much more valuable.

---

## 4. Why I'm actually interested rather than dismissing it

There's another strong signal: OpenAI now has an official developer **Showcase** and explicitly invites developers to submit projects for featuring. Current showcased projects include interactive apps, ecommerce experiences, real-estate visualization, realtime experiences and sophisticated 3D applications—not merely prompt wrappers. citeturn0search13turn0search14

So I **would allocate TEE**, but initially as an experiment:

**AUMNITY SaaS → one MCP server → one genuinely useful OpenAI Plugin/App → measure usage → only then expand.**

Not six months and £100k before validation.

A **2–4 week spike with one existing AUMNITY capability** could tell us far more cheaply whether the marketplace/distribution opportunity is real.

And importantly: **don't wait for OpenAI to pay us.** If OpenAI eventually introduces attractive builder revenue, treat that as an additional revenue channel—not the business model.

### My current TEE verdict

**OpenAI-only GPT:** 🟠 low/medium TEE  
**OpenAI App with no defensible backend:** 🟠 medium TEE  
**AUMNITY SaaS + MCP + OpenAI distribution:** 🟢 **high strategic interest**  
**Building solely for promised OpenAI revenue:** 🔴 **don't do it**

So **no, I absolutely didn't mean “OpenAI app = useless.”** I meant **don't hand OpenAI the centre of our architecture or make an uncertain builder payout the reason we build.**

And this distinction is important enough that **V001 Excel should be corrected/expanded in V002** with a dedicated **`TEE_Investment_Decision`** sheet and an **`AUMNITY_OpenAI_Product_Map`** sheet.

## 05/09/2026 18:24 — Yes, *this* partnership

Yes. I understand your question now: **not “does OpenAI partner with Microsoft/AWS?”** You mean:

> **Can a software/consulting company become an official OpenAI business partner, build OpenAI solutions for customers, co-sell them, get certification/support, and make money from implementation — like AWS/Microsoft partner ecosystems?**

### **YES. OpenAI now has exactly that.**

OpenAI has launched the **OpenAI Partner Network**. Its own description is **“Build, co-sell, and deliver AI solutions with OpenAI.”** Partners progress through **Select → Advanced → Elite**, based on sales performance, technical capability, co-selling and deployment experience. citeturn0search2turn0search4

And this is **different from the App/Plugin marketplace** we were discussing.

| Business opportunity | OpenAI status |
|---|---|
| Build an app/plugin and list it | ✅ Yes |
| Sell our own SaaS through/around it | ✅ Yes |
| Become an OpenAI implementation/consulting partner | **✅ YES** |
| Build OpenAI solutions for other businesses | **✅ YES** |
| Co-sell with OpenAI | **✅ YES — explicitly part of Partner Network** |
| Certification / enablement | **✅ YES** |
| Partner tiers | **Select / Advanced / Elite** |
| OpenAI automatically pays every marketplace-app builder | ❌ No |
| OpenAI pays us simply for becoming a partner | ❌ No — that's not what the programme means |

OpenAI's current directory already contains **AWS, Accenture, Bain, BCG, Capgemini, Cognizant, Deloitte/EY-type firms, IBM, Infosys, KPMG, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, NTT DATA, EPAM, HCLTech, Snowflake, Databricks and many specialist AI firms.** citeturn0search4

urlOpenAI Partner Networkturn0search4

### And Claude/Anthropic — YES, they moved very aggressively

This is probably what you were remembering.

Anthropic launched the **Claude Partner Network on 12 March 2026** and committed an initial **$100 million** to partner training, technical support and **joint market development**. Partner organizations could also become eligible for investment. citeturn0search3

Then by June Anthropic said **more than 40,000 firms had applied** and **10,000+ consultants had earned Claude certification**. citeturn0search7

Claude has a proper partner directory too, with firms such as Accenture designated **Global Premier** and smaller specialists at other levels. citeturn0search5turn0search6

urlClaude Partner Networkturn0search1

So **YES — there is potentially another business path here for us that is completely separate from building marketplace apps.**

### The ecosystem has *three* money paths

**1. Product company**

Build AUMNITY/UraiFlow/CGWO/etc. → expose product through OpenAI Plugin/App → customer subscribes to **our SaaS**.

**2. OpenAI services/implementation company**

Become OpenAI Partner → businesses come with problems → we design/build/deploy OpenAI solutions → **business pays us consulting/implementation/support money**.

**3. Both together — potentially the strongest**

Customer asks us to implement AI → during implementations we discover repeatable problems → instead of rebuilding every time, turn them into **AUMNITY reusable SaaS products/plugins**.

That is essentially the classic **services → reusable IP → product → marketplace** route.

---

# And your Facebook example — I think you're remembering **Friendster**, but one detail differs

Facebook launched publicly from Harvard in **2004**, rather than first appearing in 2006; 2006 was when Facebook opened registration broadly.

Before Facebook dominated, **Friendster was the leading social network**. It became huge extremely quickly and was overtaken by MySpace around 2004.

The famous rejected acquisition wasn't Microsoft: **Google reportedly offered about $30 million for Friendster in 2003**, and Friendster declined. citeturn0search69

And your larger point is much more interesting than which company made the offer:

> **How did comparatively tiny Facebook eventually beat social-networking efforts backed by Google, Microsoft and other companies with vastly more money?**

**Money wasn't the decisive moat.**

Facebook got several compounding things right: starting with a constrained real-world network (universities), identity, density of connections, engagement, developer/platform effects, distribution, and then massive network effects.

Google having billions couldn't simply order people:

> “Move your friends from Facebook to Orkut.”

A social network's value comes substantially from **everyone else already being there**.

That's why your analogy matters for what we're discussing.

OpenAI may be moving from:

**AI product**

→ **AI platform**

→ **developer ecosystem**

→ **app/plugin marketplace**

→ **services/implementation partner ecosystem**

→ **businesses building businesses on OpenAI**

And **Anthropic is pursuing essentially the same ecosystem strategy very aggressively**, including putting $100M behind its partner network. citeturn0search3

OpenAI itself made the strategy unusually explicit when announcing its Partner Network:

> “No single company can deliver every solution, in every market, for every customer.”

Its network is intended for partners **co-selling, deploying, building and connecting customers to OpenAI technology**. citeturn0search2

## This changes what I think we should research

The question isn't only:

**“Should AUMNITY build an OpenAI marketplace app?”**

There are actually **two strategic decisions**:

**AUMNITY as an OpenAI product/app developer**  
**AND**  
**AT/IPBS/etc. as an OpenAI/Claude implementation partner/business**

Those could become complementary businesses.

And **this absolutely belongs in the Excel**. V001 concentrated too much on the marketplace and missed the **Partner Network / SI / consulting / certification / co-sell economy**, which could actually be the nearer-term revenue opportunity.

I would treat **OpenAI Partner Network vs Claude Partner Network vs AWS Partner Network vs Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program** as its own serious comparative research tranche before deciding where we put TEE. memcite
